passage:
I'm Nazia, and this happened in Class 11, the month of pre-boards. We were six friends, all tired and snapping. When our group study plan fell apart, someone said, “Sahil never brings his notes on time.” It was not even true, but it was like a valve opened. Suddenly it was Sahil's fault we were behind, Sahil's fault the tuition teacher was cross.

I added a line too. Kavya frowned and said, “That's not fair,” and then went quiet. Parul stared at her phone.

We all felt lighter that week. Sahil started eating alone and never complained. I told myself he was fine. Later I saw the relief had been ours, and the weight had stayed on him.

qa.q: What did someone say about Sahil when the study plan fell apart?
qa.a: Someone said, “Sahil never brings his notes on time.”

qa.q: Why did the group feel lighter after blaming Sahil?
qa.a: The group was tired and tense before pre-boards, and blaming Sahil let the tension go, though Sahil carried the weight alone.

qa.q: What could Nazia have done when Kavya said, “That's not fair”?
qa.a: Nazia could have backed Kavya and asked the group what was really making everyone snap, instead of adding to the blame.

qa.q: What was that week like for Sahil, eating alone and never complaining?
qa.a: Sahil probably felt isolated, hurt and confused, and may have stayed quiet because arguing with five friends felt impossible.

grounding: A stressed friend group blames one member for everything, and the relief the group feels leaves the target carrying the weight alone.

passage:
Teacher's note, Class 10 B, written by Nirmala after Thursday's lab.

Five students share a lab table and have been under heavy exam pressure. This week I saw them turn on Francis, blaming him for the broken burette, the late file and a low group mark. Two students joined in eagerly. One, Ayesha, tried to change the subject. The fifth, Dev, stayed silent. Francis kept his eyes on the table and said, “Okay, sorry.”

I kept the group back and asked what each of them was worried about for the exam. Several said more than I expected. I then spoke to Francis alone, told him the blame was not his to carry, and shared the concern with the school counsellor the same afternoon.

qa.q: Which students turned on Francis during the lab?
qa.a: Five students share the lab table; two joined in blaming Francis, Ayesha tried to change the subject and Dev stayed silent.

qa.q: What does Francis saying “Okay, sorry” with eyes on the table suggest about how Francis feels?
qa.a: It suggests Francis feels ashamed and alone and has chosen not to argue with the group, perhaps hoping the blaming will pass.

qa.q: What did Nirmala do that turned the group's attention from blame to the real problem?
qa.a: Nirmala kept the group back and asked what each student was worried about for the exam, so the pressure was named instead of a person.

qa.q: What might Dev, the silent fifth student, have been thinking during the blaming?
qa.a: Dev may have felt uncomfortable and guilty but afraid to speak against the others, or worried about becoming the next target.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a lab group under exam stress blaming one member, and how the teacher separated the stress from the target and involved the counsellor.

passage:
Yash, you think your friend group is falling apart before exams? Listen to your Reena bua. I've seen it.
In Class 10, there were five of us, very close. Then board exams came. Everyone was scared, tempers short. And somehow it all became Kamla's fault. She was late to our study group: Kamla's fault. The notes got lost: Kamla. Someone's mother shouted: must be because of Kamla.
And you know what? Each time we blamed her, the rest of us felt lighter. We laughed more.
Kamla just got quieter. She started studying alone in the library. None of us asked why.
After the exams, she moved schools. I still have a photo of the five of us. I look at her face in it.

qa.q: How many friends were in young Reena's group?
qa.a: There were five of them.

qa.q: How did blaming Kamla make the rest of the group feel?
qa.a: Each time they blamed her they felt lighter and relieved, laughing more while their exam fear eased.

qa.q: At what point in the story could someone have made a different choice?
qa.a: When Kamla started studying alone, one of them could have asked her why and admitted the blame was unfair.

qa.q: How might Kamla have felt that year?
qa.a: She probably felt lonely and hurt, carrying the group's stress alone until she moved schools.

grounding: An elder recalls how her friend group, stressed by exams, blamed one member for everything, relieving their tension while she carried it alone.

passage:
Two hours before the inter-school dance competition, the power went out in the green room, and one costume was missing.
“Hansa, you packed the bag,” said Priya.
“I packed what you gave me!”
“And you're always slow in the second step,” added Neha.
Usha, the group leader, felt her panic turn into something sharper. “Honestly, Hansa, everything goes wrong around you.”
The others nodded. Somehow, blaming Hansa made the room feel calmer. They started fixing their makeup by phone torchlight, joking again.
Hansa sat in the corner, holding the empty bag. Nobody sat with her.
The missing costume turned up in Neha's own bag ten minutes before the show. Nobody said sorry.

qa.q: Where did the missing costume turn up?
qa.a: It turned up in Neha's own bag.

qa.q: What did Usha feel when her panic turned sharp?
qa.a: She felt stressed and panicky, and blaming Hansa gave her and the group a sense of relief.

qa.q: What went wrong in the green room, and what could fix it?
qa.a: Under stress, the group made Hansa carry every problem; checking all the bags calmly and saying sorry to her would have been fairer.

qa.q: How might Hansa have felt sitting in the corner?
qa.a: She likely felt hurt, isolated and unfairly blamed, holding the empty bag with nobody beside her.

grounding: Shows a stressed teen dance group blaming one member for everything, which relieves their tension while she carries it alone.

passage:
After losing the colony cricket final, the team sat on the steps outside the Andheri building, sweaty and silent.
“Yogesh dropped that catch,” Omkar said finally. “That was the match.”
“And the two byes,” added Sahil.
“And he was late for the toss,” said someone else.
It was strange how good it felt. With every “Yogesh,” the heavy feeling in Omkar's chest got lighter. Nobody mentioned Omkar's own run-out, or Sahil's bad over.
Yogesh sat one step lower, pulling at his gloves. He didn't argue. He just said, “Sorry, guys,” very quietly.
Walking home, Omkar replayed his own run-out and felt uncomfortable, but he didn't turn around.

qa.q: What did Omkar say Yogesh dropped?
qa.a: He said Yogesh dropped that catch.

qa.q: Why did Omkar's chest feel lighter as they blamed Yogesh?
qa.a: He felt relieved, because blaming Yogesh moved the attention away from his own run-out and the team's loss.

qa.q: What could Omkar do to put things right?
qa.a: He could admit his own run-out to the team and tell Yogesh the loss wasn't only his fault.

qa.q: How might Yogesh have felt sitting one step lower?
qa.a: He probably felt ashamed and alone, carrying the whole team's loss and apologising quietly.

grounding: Shows a teen cricket team, stressed by a loss, blaming one member for everything, relieving the group while he carries it alone.

passage:
"We lost the quiz because Saurabh buzzed too early."
"And the notes didn't get printed because Saurabh forgot the pen drive."
"And the lab slot got cancelled..."
"That was the teacher, Tejas," Meera said.
"Yeah, but Saurabh was supposed to confirm it." Tejas laughed, and the others laughed too. It felt good, somehow, like letting air out of a tyre. Boards were three weeks away and everyone's stomach was in knots.
Saurabh sat at the end of the bench, peeling the label off his water bottle. "I did confirm it. I have the message."
"Sure, bro."
"Can we not do this every day?" Saurabh said quietly.
Nobody answered. Meera looked at Tejas. Tejas looked at his phone. The quiz, the notes, the lab slot: when he thought about it, only the quiz was even partly Saurabh's.

qa.q: How far away were the boards?
qa.a: Boards were three weeks away.

qa.q: Why did blaming Saurabh feel good to Tejas?
qa.a: Tejas was anxious about boards, and laughing at Saurabh let that tension out "like letting air out of a tyre".

qa.q: What could Tejas do now that he sees most of it wasn't Saurabh's fault?
qa.a: Say so to the group, drop the jokes, and check with Saurabh privately; one voice can stop the daily blame.

qa.q: What is it like for Saurabh to hear this every day?
qa.a: Saurabh feels hurt and worn down, carrying the group's exam stress alone, as "Can we not do this every day?" shows.

grounding: Shows a stressed friend group before exams piling every problem onto one member, which relieves their tension while he carries it alone.
